extracted.intended_audience: parties and counsel in Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB) inter partes proceedings
extracted.subtask_short: TTAB discovery in inter partes proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on disclosures and discovery procedures for inter partes trademark proceedings before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, covering discovery conferences, initial and expert disclosures, timing, scope, duties, and remedial measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Federal Rules to Board Proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR § 2.120(a)(1): Wherever appropriate, the provisions of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure relating to disclosure and discovery shall apply in opposition, cancellation, interference and concurrent use registration proceedings except as otherwise provided in this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board applies the Federal Rules (notably Fed. R. Civ. P. 26) in modified form; the Board will specify deadlines for a discovery conference, opening/closing dates for taking discovery, and deadlines for initial and expert disclosures. The disclosure regime was adopted for proceedings commencing on or after Nov. 1, 2007, to promote early exchange of information, reduce unfair surprise, and encourage efficient resolution (including ACR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of Discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Through disclosures and discovery devices a party may ascertain the facts underlying its adversary's case; discovery may lead to settlement, simplify issues, reveal basis for summary judgment or additional claims/defenses, and permit stipulations and preparation for trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery enables proposing stipulations of fact, procedures for introducing evidence, narrowing issues, or pursuing Accelerated Case Resolution (ACR). Initial and expert disclosures are intended to obviate the need for traditional discovery to obtain 'basic information.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery Conference Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery conference shall occur no later than the opening of the discovery period, and the parties must discuss the subjects set forth in Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f) and any subjects set forth in the Board’s institution order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For cases commenced on/after Nov. 1, 2007, parties are required to hold a discovery conference to discuss Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f) topics and institution-order subjects. A Board Interlocutory Attorney or Administrative Trademark Judge may participate upon timely request. Parties are not required to file a written report of the conference unless they seek to alter disclosure/discovery obligations or are directed to file one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects to be Discussed at Discovery Conference
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must consider: (1) the nature and basis of their respective claims and defenses; (2) the possibility of settling or narrowing claims/defenses; (3) arrangements relating to disclosures, discovery and introduction of evidence at trial; and any topics listed in the institution order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion should include whether to seek mediation/arbitration, consideration of the Board's ACR process, whether to alter disclosure/discovery procedures or the Standard Protective Order, limitations on disclosures, stipulations of fact, and efficient options for introducing discovery-produced material at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing, Deadlines, and Exceptions for Discovery Conference
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery conference must take place by the deadline set in the Board’s institution order (or any approved extension) and no later than the opening of the discovery period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant is in default, or a Rule 12 motion or counterclaim has been filed, the obligation to hold the conference is stayed until pleadings are resolved; the Board will reset deadlines then. The Board is generally unlikely to extend the discovery-conference deadline for settlement discussions. The Board can order parties to hold a conference sua sponte or on motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format of Discovery Conference and Board Participation Procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The parties' discovery conference may be in person or by other means (e.g., telephone). If any party wants a Board professional to participate, the party must call the Board attorney or file a request through ESTTA no later than ten days prior to the deadline for the conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board participation is by telephone, is encouraged where pro se litigants are involved, and the participating attorney/judge may expand or reduce subjects to be discussed. If no request is made, the Board will assume the conference occurred by the deadline; mere settlement discussions do not substitute for a full conference.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Required Filing of a Discovery/Disclosure Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike the Federal Rules, the parties do not have to file a disclosure/discovery plan with the Board following their discovery conference, unless they are seeking leave by motion or stipulation to alter standard deadlines or obligations, or unless directed to do so by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should still discuss reciprocal obligations and progress even after the conference, especially if they enter stipulations altering obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Disclosures — Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial disclosures must be made no later than thirty days after the opening of the discovery period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party must make initial disclosures prior to seeking discovery, absent Board-approved stipulation or motion. A party failing to make initial disclosures may face a motion to compel and discovery sanctions; and generally a party may not file for summary judgment until it has made its initial disclosures (with limited exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Disclosures — Required Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Per Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1): (i) the name and, if known, address and telephone of each individual likely to have discoverable information and the subjects of that information that the disclosing party may use to support its claims or defenses; (ii) a copy — or a description by category and location — of all documents, electronically stored information, and tangible things in the disclosing party's possession, custody, or control that it may use to support its claims or defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsections (iii) and (iv) of Rule 26(a)(1)(A) do not apply to Board proceedings. Pertinent ESI must be identified. If a trial witness is identified, the subject matter the witness is likely to have discoverable information about must be provided, along with any known contact information. A party may either provide the location of identified documents or produce them; the Board encourages actual exchange of copies rather than mere identification of location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and Limitation of Initial Disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A party is not obligated to disclose every witness, document, or thing that may have discoverable information; only those witnesses, documents, and things having discoverable information that the disclosing party may use to support its claims or defenses must be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial disclosures are intended to prompt routine disclosure of basic information, not to substitute for comprehensive discovery. Discovery in Board proceedings should be more limited than in district court due to limited TTAB jurisdiction; parties may, with Board approval, stipulate to more expansive reciprocal disclosures to reduce formal discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Supplement Disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must supplement disclosures when required under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e); there is no concept of priority relieving a party of its obligation to make or supplement disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party remains obligated to supplement even if it has not received supplementation from adverse parties. See TBMP § 408.03 for further information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Initial Disclosures at Summary Judgment and Trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial written disclosures and initial disclosures of documents are treated like responses to discovery requests insofar as they may be used in support of or in opposition to a motion for summary judgment and may, at trial, be introduced by notice of reliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because initial disclosures can be used as evidence, parties should ensure disclosures are accurate and timely. A party failing to make initial disclosures may be subject to sanctions including exclusion or motions to compel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and Remedies for Failure to Provide Initial Disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A party failing to make initial disclosures may be subject to a motion to compel and ultimately a motion for discovery sanctions; a party may not file a motion for summary judgment until it has made its initial disclosures (except for issue preclusion or lack of Board jurisdiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies and sanctions are further discussed in TBMP § 411 and the duty to cooperate provisions in TBMP § 408.01(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert Disclosures — Governing Rule and Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of expert testimony must occur in the manner and sequence provided in Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2), unless alternate directions are provided by the Board. Absent order, expert disclosures are due 30 days before the close of discovery (or timing per Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 when no Board order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party generally must decide within the discovery period whether it plans to use an expert; if an expert is retained after the deadline, the party must promptly file a motion for leave to use the expert. The Board may set or reset deadlines and may suspend proceedings to permit expert-limited discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert Disclosures — Written Report Content (Retained Experts)
rubrics_metrics.description: For retained or specially employed experts, the written report must contain: (i) a complete statement of all opinions and the basis and reasons for them; (ii) the facts or data considered; (iii) any exhibits used to summarize/support them; (iv) the witness's qualifications, including publications in the previous 10 years; (v) a list of other cases in the previous 4 years in which the witness testified as an expert; and (vi) a statement of the compensation to be paid for the study and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These requirements follow Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2)(B); parties are expected to cooperate in exchanging information about testifying experts and to discuss stipulations to facilitate expert exchange and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert Disclosures — Summary Disclosures (Non-report Experts)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the witness is not required to provide a written report, the disclosure must state: (i) the subject matter on which the witness is expected to present evidence under Rules 702, 703, or 705; and (ii) a summary of the facts and opinions to which the witness is expected to testify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2)(C); disclosures must be supplemented per Rule 26(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board Notification and Handling of Expert Disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Any party disclosing plans to use an expert must notify the Board that it has made the required disclosure (but should not file copies of materials provided to adverse parties). The Board may suspend proceedings to allow for expert discovery and/or set deadlines for rebuttal experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspension orders may leave unchanged or reset rebuttal deadlines. The Board decides on case-by-case basis how to handle late identification of experts; prompt disclosure and a motion for leave are required for late experts but do not guarantee admission of testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late Identification of Experts and Motions for Leave
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party decides after the expert-disclosure deadline that it needs to rely on expert testimony, the party must file a motion for leave to use the expert at trial; prompt disclosure after the deadline is required but does not ensure the expert will be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will decide late-identification issues case-by-case and may or may not permit late expert testimony; parties should plan expert retention and disclosure timing to allow adequate opposing discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of Electronically Stored Information (ESI) in Disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pertinent information under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1) stored in digital or electronic form must also be identified in initial disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See TBMP § 402.02 for further information regarding discovery of electronically stored information and any limitations or procedures applicable in Board proceedings.
